About this document

This document provides the teaching content for Mathematical and Statistical
Modelling Years 12–13 of the New Zealand Curriculum. Equivalent for
Te Marautanga o Aotearoa is being published separately.

Progress and assessment information for Mathematical and Statistical Modelling
Years 12–13 is still in development. Once that is completed, Mathematical and
Statistical Modelling Years 12–13 is proposed to be made by the Minister of
Education as a National Curriculum Statement under section 90(1)(a) of the
Education and Training Act 2020.

It is proposed that, once made and published in the New Zealand Gazette, schools
who offer Mathematical and Statistical Modelling Years 12–13 will be required to start
using it in Year 12 from 1 January 2029, and in Year 13 from 1 January 2030.

This document will be replaced with the official version made under the Act and
published in the New Zealand Gazette once that has occurred.




Mathematical and Statistical Modelling | Years 12–13 | October 2026                      Page 2

Purpose statement                                                  Ānō me he whare pūngāwerewere.   Behold, it is like the web of a spider.




  Students are taught mathematical and statistical concepts for investigating and
  solving problems to enable future innovation. They are taught practical
  applications such as mathematical modelling, data analysis, and interpretation of
  results. They are also taught how to apply reasoning, solve problems, and
  critically evaluate models and solutions.


Through the study of Mathematical and Statistical Modelling, students are taught
mathematical, statistical, and probabilistic concepts, representations and methods.
They explore context-specific information to analyse problems, identify patterns and
relationships, and develop solutions in both tangible and theoretical contexts.

Mathematical and Statistical Modelling provides students with the knowledge and
practices to use mathematical language, symbols, equations, graphs and data
visualisations to represent, analyse, and communicate information in written form.
This disciplinary knowledge enables students to make informed decisions, evaluate
risk, and examine the integrity of data and the suitability of solutions.

As students’ progress through Years 12–13 Mathematical and Statistical Modelling,
they are supported to develop their ability to evaluate data, models, and conclusions,
and use critical reasoning. They consider validity, limitations, and ethical implications,
bridging theoretical mathematical and statistical reasoning with practical application.


  Mathematical and Statistical Modelling strengthens knowledge and capabilities
  for industry pathways and leads to careers in mathematics and statistics, and
  related fields including computer science, biology, business, psychology,
  economics, and health sciences.

The teaching of all knowledge and practices is compulsory. Schools can determine
how learning is organised across the year, including integrating content from multiple
elements and strands where this supports coherence and depth. Examples within the
teaching sequence and contexts in brackets signified with ‘e.g.’ are provided as
guidance only; provided the intended knowledge and practices are met, schools and
teachers may substitute contexts and examples that better reflect local environments,
iwi and hapū connections, student interests, and teacher expertise.

Disciplinary writing is included in the teaching sequence to provide clarity about what
subject-specific literacy is to be taught. Disciplinary writing is organised into a
knowledge component that is consistent across all year levels and a practice
component that is sequenced across years.
